1.title: Identity and Access Management
1.text: Welcome to Module fifteen: Identity and Access Management. It covers the exam area Security Operations. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do seven things. The identity life cycle. Federation and single sign-on. Account types. Multifactor authentication. Access control models. Password concepts. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Security Operations (twenty-seven percent). Exam format: up to ninety questions in ninety minutes; a score of seven hundred fifty on a scale of one hundred to nine hundred passes. Validated against: the official Comp T I A Security plus S Y zero eight oh one V eight exam objectives.

1.title: The identity life cycle
1.text: The identity life cycle. Provisioning or deprovisioning. Create accounts when people join and remove or disable them when they leave or change roles (prompt deprovisioning prevents stale accounts). Permissions assignments and implications. Grant only what is needed; broad rights raise risk. Identity proofing. Verify that a person is who they claim before creating an account. Access review. Regularly check who has which rights and remove excess (fights privilege creep).

1.title: The identity life cycle, continued
1.text: The identity life cycle. The figure shows this: Identity life cycle: prove identity, provision, review, change, deprovision.

1.title: Federation and single sign-on
1.text: Federation and single sign-on. Federation. Trust between organizations so users can use one identity across them. Single sign-on. Sign in once and reach many applications. sam el. X M L-based standard to pass authentication between an identity provider and an application (common for web S S O at work). L D A P (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol). Lightweight Directory Access Protocol: query and manage a directory such as Active Directory. oh auth. Open standard for authorization: lets one app access another on your behalf without sharing your password. Exam tip: sam el equals authentication across domains. oh auth equals delegated authorization (access to resources). L D A P equals directory access. An identity provider (I D P) authenticates; the service provider relies on it.

1.title: Account types
1.text: Account types. User. Normal day-to-day access. Privileged. Administrator rights: global (whole environment) or local (one system). Needs extra protection. Service. Used by applications and services, not people; avoid interactive sign-in, rotate secrets. Third-party. Accounts for vendors or partners: time-limit and monitor. Emergency access (break-glass). Highly privileged, stored securely, used only in emergencies, heavily monitored.

1.title: Multifactor authentication (MFA)
1.text: Multifactor authentication. M F A combines two or more factors: something you know, have, are, plus (sometimes) where you are or what you do. Hard token. Physical device (key fob, security key). Soft token. Software on a phone (authenticator app). Biometrics. Fingerprint, face, iris. One-time password (O T P). A code valid once (time-based or counter-based). Backup code. Single-use recovery codes.

1.title: Multifactor authentication (MFA), continued
1.text: Multifactor authentication. The figure shows this: Authentication factors: know, have, are. Exam tip: A password plus a P I N is not M F A (both are something you know). Password plus a security key is M F A. Store backup codes safely.

1.title: Access control models
1.text: Access control models. Discretionary (D A C). The owner decides who gets access. Mandatory (M A C). The system enforces access by labels and clearances (military style). Role-based (R B A C). By job role. Rule-based. By rules (for example firewall rules, "no access from outside the office"). Time-based. Allowed only in certain hours. Just-in-time (J I T). Temporary elevated access, only when needed.

1.title: Access management
1.text: Access management. Authentication, and policies: logical (technical) such as groups and permissions, and administrative (business) such as hiring and approval rules.

1.title: Password concepts
1.text: Password concepts. Passkey. Passwordless sign-in using a cryptographic key pair; resists phishing. Password managers. Create and store unique strong passwords. Passwordless. Sign in with something other than a password (passkey, biometrics, security key). Best practices. Length (longer is better), complexity, no reuse, expiration and age (modern guidance favors changing only after compromise), compromised credential monitoring, account auditing, policy report. Exam tip: Length beats complexity. Never reuse passwords. Passkeys are phishing-resistant. Just-in-time access reduces standing privileges.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Fabrikam Outdoors wants staff to sign in once and reach many cloud apps using the company identity provider. Which concept fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Single sign-on with federation. S S O lets users authenticate once, and federation extends the trusted identity to other services.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A user must enter a password and then a six-digit code from an authenticator app. Which factors are used? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Something you know and something you have. The password is knowledge and the app code from a phone is a possession factor.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A vendor needs administrator rights for two hours to fix a system. Which approach reduces standing privilege? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Just-in-time access. Just-in-time grants temporary elevated access only when needed.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A web app wants to read a user's calendar from another service without getting the user's password. Which standard fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: oh auth. oh auth provides delegated authorization without sharing credentials.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. After a quarterly review, managers remove access that employees no longer need after moving teams. Which problem is this addressing? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Privilege creep. Access reviews remove accumulated permissions, which is privilege creep.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A company sets a rule that a payroll system can only be used from the office between eight and six. Which models are combined? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Time-based and rule-based. The rule limits by hours (time-based) and by location through rules (rule-based).

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is identity proofing? Answer: Verifying that a person is who they claim to be before creating an account. Question two. sam el or oh auth: which is for authentication across domains? Answer: sam el. Question three. Name the five account types in the objectives. Answer: User, privileged, service, third-party and emergency access.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Name three M F A methods. Answer: For example hard token, soft token, biometrics, one-time password, backup code. Question five. What is a passkey? Answer: A passwordless credential based on a cryptographic key pair. Question six. Which access control model uses labels and clearances? Answer: Mandatory access control.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Life cycle: identity proofing, provisioning, permissions, access reviews, deprovisioning. Federation: S S O; sam el (authentication), oh auth (delegated authorization), L D A P (directory). Accounts: user, privileged (global or local), service, third-party, emergency (break-glass). M F A: hard and soft tokens, biometrics, O T P, backup codes; two different factor types. Models: D A C, M A C, role-based, rule-based, time-based, just-in-time. Passwords: passkeys, password managers, passwordless; length, no reuse, monitor compromised credentials. In the next module, we continue the course.
